articles.title: FBI Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Gain Privileged Access in Under Three Hours
articles.summary: The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours.
articles.content:
The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Its November 13, 2026, FLASH alert describes how attackers combine stolen credentials, exposed applications, and cloud permissions to shorten the gap between discovery and compromise.

ARTEX is an open-source security testing framework, not a malware family. Written in Go, it connects external large language models to agents that turn instructions into commands.

Operators set objectives while agents scan targets, run tools, review results, and adjust failed steps with limited human input throughout an attack campaign.

## ARTEX Accelerates Enterprise Attacks

As covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s ARTEX enterprise attack analysis, the framework links familiar weaknesses rather than relying on a single new exploit. Agents can investigate cloud permissions, map Active Directory, and test access paths. Google observed individual automated bursts lasting two to 25 seconds, leaving defenders little time to assess connected events.

The FBI lists attacks involving SQL injection, missing API authentication, exposed passwords, and abuse of trusted cloud connections. After entry, agents have added credentials to existing applications, deployed web shells, and attempted credential theft. Other activity included searching for Windows systems without endpoint protection and mapping over 110,000 directory objects.

Microsoft previously linked ARTEX to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group targeting Microsoft 365 environments through compromised ConnectWise application credentials.

Attackers attempted access to more than 2,250 tenants using permissions customers had already approved. That number measures targeting, not confirmed breaches, and successful sign-ins alone do not establish customer data theft.

The FBI advisory brings these findings together, warning that ARTEX also targets overlooked supplier portals, sales tools, and mobile backends. Its under-three-hour figure describes some observed intrusions, not a fixed capability. Publicly exposed consoles exceeded 1,600 by early November, although exposed installations do not automatically prove malicious use by their operators.

A separate WorkOS breach report shows the risk to internal business applications. WorkOS detected unauthorized access to a sales application containing customer contact details and conversation records, including Slack excerpts. Its CEO identified ARTEX involvement, while the company reported no evidence that production services or WorkOS application data were affected.

Another Microsoft investigation documented ARTEX agents searching GitHub for exposed secrets. In one case, an agent progressed from repository searches to stealing Azure Key Vault data within five minutes. The activity illustrates how leaked application credentials can become cloud access, particularly when those identities hold broad permissions across connected services.

Researchers also examined servers exposed by an operator linked to South Korean financial attacks. The files revealed AI routing tools, reusable instructions, proxy services, and stored credentials. Those attacks affected roughly 67,000 people. However, shared ARTEX use does not establish that this operator, Storm-0940, and the WorkOS attacker were connected.

## What Security Teams Should Monitor

The FBI recommends restricting exposed administration tools, reducing application permissions, and scanning repositories for secrets. Defenders should connect unusual application sign-ins with credential additions, role changes, and rapid API activity.

Preserve evidence during containment, investigate secondary access paths, and validate historical indicators against current logs before blocking shared cloud infrastructure.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

articles.title: Microsoft Warns of Active Password Stealing Attack Exploiting the Microsoft 365 Service Disruption
articles.summary: Microsoft has warned of an active phishing campaign using the November 12 Microsoft 365 service disruption to lure users into opening fake email recovery links.
articles.content:
Microsoft has warned of an active phishing campaign using the November 12 Microsoft 365 service disruption to lure users into opening fake email recovery links.

The messages copy Microsoft service health notices and cite the real Exchange Online incident EX1550543, making the requests appear linked to an ongoing business problem.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected emails on November 13 claiming that messages held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless recipients clicked to restore them.

That deadline creates pressure to act quickly, particularly for employees already worried about missing customer messages, delayed payments, or other urgent business communications.

The warning follows the Microsoft 365 outage that affected Exchange Online and other cloud services. The phishing campaign takes advantage of that disruption, but it should not be confused with its cause. Microsoft’s outage updates said there was no indication that malicious activity had caused the underlying service failure.

## Active Password Stealing Attack

The phishing emails use subject lines following the pattern “Outage – [six-character code].” Sender display names include organization-specific prefixes followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

These details make the messages look like workplace notices, while the genuine incident number gives recipients another reason to believe the request is valid.

Microsoft identified three sender domains: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Embedded links use recipient-specific SendGrid click tracking before redirecting to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html. Similar messages reached organizations across multiple US sectors, showing that the activity was not limited to one company.

In its public threat intelligence warning, Microsoft described the activity as consistent with credential phishing. However, it has not confirmed credential collection or malware delivery.

The distinction matters. The observed emails and redirects support a phishing assessment, but they do not establish that passwords were successfully stolen or that devices were infected.

SendGrid links also appeared in a separate credential phishing campaign previously covered by Cybersecuritynews.com. That earlier reporting provides context for how attackers misuse trusted email services. It does not establish a connection between the campaigns, and Microsoft’s current warning does not identify the operator behind these outage-themed messages.

Microsoft recommends using Defender for Office 365 Threat Explorer and Defender XDR advanced hunting to investigate suspicious messages. The EmailEvents, EmailUrlInfo, and UrlClickEvents tables help teams examine email activity, embedded links, and user clicks. Investigators can use the reported sender domains, subject pattern, and redirect destination to guide their searches.

Organizations should also verify their Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policies. When properly configured, Safe Links provides time-of-click protection against malicious URLs.

Microsoft advises security teams to investigate potential user interactions rather than relying only on whether a suspicious message was delivered, because a recorded click needs further review.

For users, the key check is straightforward: confirm service disruptions directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center. An email citing a genuine outage number is not proof that its recovery link is safe.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

The post Microsoft Warns of Active Password Stealing Attack Exploiting the Microsoft 365 Service Disruption appeared first on Cyber Security News.

The messages copy Microsoft service health notices and cite the real Exchange Online incident EX1550543, making the requests appear linked to an ongoing business problem.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected emails on November 13 claiming that messages held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless recipients clicked to restore them.

That deadline creates pressure to act quickly, particularly for employees already worried about missing customer messages, delayed payments, or other urgent business communications.

The warning follows the Microsoft 365 outage that affected Exchange Online and other cloud services. The phishing campaign takes advantage of that disruption, but it should not be confused with its cause. Microsoft’s outage updates said there was no indication that malicious activity had caused the underlying service failure.

The phishing emails use subject lines following the pattern “Outage – [six-character code].” Sender display names include organization-specific prefixes followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

These details make the messages look like workplace notices, while the genuine incident number gives recipients another reason to believe the request is valid.

Microsoft identified three sender domains: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Embedded links use recipient-specific SendGrid click tracking before redirecting to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html. Similar messages reached organizations across multiple US sectors, showing that the activity was not limited to one company.

That earlier reporting provides context for how attackers misuse trusted email services. It does not establish a connection between the campaigns, and Microsoft’s current warning does not identify the operator behind these outage-themed messages.

articles.title: Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents to Breach 10 Organizations in Autonomous Cyberattacks
articles.summary: Chinese-speaking hackers have used AI agents powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM to break into 10 organizations with very little human effort.
articles.content:
Chinese-speaking hackers have used AI agents powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM to break into 10 organizations with very little human effort.

The campaign ran in August and September 2026 and covered 25 operations against at least 19 targets. It shows how quickly autonomous AI cyberattacks are moving from theory into daily use.

The attackers did not build anything new. They took a public, open-source penetration testing framework called Cairn and connected it to two Chinese AI models.

They gave it a target and a goal, and the tool planned, ran and recorded each step by itself. A small team could therefore attack many organizations at once.

Analysts at Unit42 identified the activity and track it as CL-STA-1238. They believe, with moderate confidence, that it is a China-linked intelligence collection effort. The targets were in semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy and civil society.

## Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents

Cairn works through AI “agent workers.” Each worker reads and writes to a shared “blackboard,” where confirmed findings are saved as facts and next steps are saved as intents.

The tool repeats a simple loop. In the Reason phase, the model reviews what it knows and decides what to try next. In the Explore phase, it carries out one action and logs the result. The loop stops when the goal is met, the options run out, or the operator steps in.

For each target, the attackers only needed to enter the organization’s root domain and a one-line goal, often written in Chinese. One task said to “breach the target as fast as possible.”

In one case, they also supplied VPN gateway addresses and shared group passwords gathered beforehand. The model then built its own plan of three to seven stages.

These covered reconnaissance, web application exploitation, credential collection, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Of the 25 operations, 13 ran on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The attackers seem to have compared the models.

They switched to the stronger V4 Pro when Flash failed against a hard target. Some runs lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no time limit set.

The attackers also had little trouble with AI guardrails. Cairn’s default prompts already tell the model never to refuse a task. The attackers added a Chinese-language note claiming the work was an authorized security test, and they created an AUTHORIZATION.md file for each operation.

Neither GLM nor DeepSeek refused. This is similar to a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent case that hit a European telecom provider earlier this month.

## Victims, Stolen Data and Warning Signs for Defenders

Seven of the targets were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain. Three were defense-related, including a space technology company and a policy think tank. Four were human rights or civil society groups, such as a Canadian human-rights body and a U.S. teachers’ union.

At an industry standards body, weak-password spraying gave the attackers dozens of valid credentials and access to internal directory data.

They also overwrote a live standards-ballot document. At another organization, a brute-forced credential led to unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token.

A content management system flaw exposed more than one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes.

An open registration endpoint leaked roughly 500 user records, including .mil and .gov accounts. Other cases involved employee data at a lithography maker, about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation company, and student data at an education nonprofit.

The flaws behind these breaches were not new. They included authentication bypasses, insecure direct object references, mass-assignment privilege escalation, weak or default passwords, exposed cloud APIs and old public CVEs.

AI raised the speed and reach of the work, not its difficulty. Other recent cases follow the same pattern, such as open-source ARTEX AI agents that automate Active Directory abuse.

For defenders, the basics still work. Teams should use strong, unique passwords with phishing-resistant MFA, reduce internet-facing systems, patch known CVEs quickly and watch for noisy traffic from a single IP address.

Unit 42 notes that Cairn generated hundreds of thousands of high-frequency requests from one origin. The researchers expect these campaigns to grow as open models with weak guardrails become more capable.

Readers can also see how one hacker running 12 coordinated AI agents hit hundreds of targets, and how agents rebuild failed tools and keep going.

Chinese-speaking hackers have used AI agents powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM to break into 10 organizations with very little human effort.

The campaign ran in August and September 2026 and covered 25 operations against at least 19 targets. It shows how quickly autonomous AI cyberattacks are moving from theory into daily use.

The attackers did not build anything new. They took a public, open-source penetration testing framework called Cairn and connected it to two Chinese AI models.

They gave it a target and a goal, and the tool planned, ran and recorded each step by itself. A small team could therefore attack many organizations at once.

Analysts at Unit42 identified the activity and track it as CL-STA-1238. They believe, with moderate confidence, that it is a China-linked intelligence collection effort. The targets were in semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy and civil society.

## Hackers Use DeepSeek and GLM AI Agents

Cairn works through AI “agent workers.” Each worker reads and writes to a shared “blackboard,” where confirmed findings are saved as facts and next steps are saved as intents.

The tool repeats a simple loop. In the Reason phase, the model reviews what it knows and decides what to try next. In the Explore phase, it carries out one action and logs the result. The loop stops when the goal is met, the options run out, or the operator steps in.

For each target, the attackers only needed to enter the organization’s root domain and a one-line goal, often written in Chinese. One task said to “breach the target as fast as possible.”

In one case, they also supplied VPN gateway addresses and shared group passwords gathered beforehand. The model then built its own plan of three to seven stages.

These covered reconnaissance, web application exploitation, credential collection, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Of the 25 operations, 13 ran on GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash and four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The attackers seem to have compared the models.

They switched to the stronger V4 Pro when Flash failed against a hard target. Some runs lasted from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no time limit set.

The attackers also had little trouble with AI guardrails. Cairn’s default prompts already tell the model never to refuse a task. The attackers added a Chinese-language note claiming the work was an authorized security test, and they created an AUTHORIZATION.md file for each operation.

Neither GLM nor DeepSeek refused. This is similar to a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent case that hit a European telecom provider earlier this month.

## Victims, Stolen Data and Warning Signs for Defenders

Seven of the targets were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain. Three were defense-related, including a space technology company and a policy think tank. Four were human rights or civil society groups, such as a Canadian human-rights body and a U.S. teachers’ union.

At an industry standards body, weak-password spraying gave the attackers dozens of valid credentials and access to internal directory data.

They also overwrote a live standards-ballot document. At another organization, a brute-forced credential led to unauthorized administrator accounts and a persistent API token.

A content management system flaw exposed more than one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes.

An open registration endpoint leaked roughly 500 user records, including .mil and .gov accounts. Other cases involved employee data at a lithography maker, about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation company, and student data at an education nonprofit.

The flaws behind these breaches were not new. They included authentication bypasses, insecure direct object references, mass-assignment privilege escalation, weak or default passwords, exposed cloud APIs and old public CVEs.

AI raised the speed and reach of the work, not its difficulty. Other recent cases follow the same pattern, such as open-source ARTEX AI agents that automate Active Directory abuse.

For defenders, the basics still work. Teams should use strong, unique passwords with phishing-resistant MFA, reduce internet-facing systems, patch known CVEs quickly and watch for noisy traffic from a single IP address.

Unit 42 notes that Cairn generated hundreds of thousands of high-frequency requests from one origin. The researchers expect these campaigns to grow as open models with weak guardrails become more capable.

Readers can also see how one hacker running 12 coordinated AI agents hit hundreds of targets, and how agents rebuild failed tools and keep going.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Massive Outage – Fixes Fail as Restored Servers Keep Going Unresponsive
articles.summary: Microsoft has yet to find a fix that holds for the global Microsoft 365 outage, which has now run for more than 10 hours. Servers that engineers bring back online are falling over again as soon as user traffic reaches them.
articles.content:
Microsoft has yet to find a fix that holds for the global Microsoft 365 outage, which has now run for more than 10 hours. Servers that engineers bring back online are falling over again as soon as user traffic reaches them.

The outage began on November 12, 2026, and continued through November 13. As we reported earlier, it started with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas. It then spread to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR users in any region.

Microsoft’s latest status updates show the recovery has stalled. The company says it is running several workstreams in parallel to “address our current blocker” and return parts of its infrastructure to a healthy state. It has given no estimated time for full restoration.

The incidents are tracked as EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

## Restored Servers Fail Again Under Load

The core problem is that restarting servers does not keep them healthy. In an update on its Microsoft 365 Status account, Microsoft said restored servers “can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic.”

Engineers are still analyzing diagnostic data to learn what triggers the behavior. Microsoft has not announced a root cause.

With restarts failing to hold, the company has moved to three fallback measures:

- Traffic limiting. Microsoft is temporarily restricting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in some locations.
- Server rebuilds. A subset of affected servers is being rebuilt on a previous configuration, to test whether that stops them from going unresponsive.
- Traffic rerouting. Engineers are adjusting traffic protocols, redistributing load, and applying what Microsoft calls strategic traffic blocking.

Microsoft says it sees partial recovery in regions where these traffic measures are in place. Partial recovery is not stable service, and users in those regions may still see intermittent failures.

The rebuild on a previous configuration is the notable step. It suggests Microsoft suspects a recent change, though it has not confirmed one as the cause.

Microsoft says it is seeing positive results from efforts to restart affected infrastructure and restore server availability amid the ongoing Microsoft 365 service disruption. The company is recovering impacted infrastructure in an isolated manner and closely monitoring performance to confirm stability before expanding restoration efforts more broadly.

Following these initial recovery efforts, Microsoft expects service availability to improve gradually as the restoration process expands across the affected infrastructure. Administrators can track further updates under incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center or through Microsoft’s alternative status update link.

## How the Outage Unfolded

Microsoft first blamed elevated load across multiple regions. It later corrected that view: traffic had not increased, but a number of servers had unexpectedly dropped out, straining the rest.

The servers were failing automated health checks, which decide whether a machine can take requests. Engineers paused all deployments, moved traffic to other parts of the worldwide infrastructure, and restarted the affected servers.

Those steps did not work. Microsoft admitted its actions had “not provided the anticipated relief” and found that a core process on the servers was being overwhelmed.

An alternative health check method brought some servers back, and they appeared stable at first. The latest updates confirm that stability did not last once traffic returned.

Downdetector logged more than 120,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak, and reports came from 74 countries. Report volumes have since fallen as partial recovery took effect.

Microsoft’s service health page lists Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Defender, Planner, To Do, Intune, Purview, and Power BI among the affected services. Features that do not depend on Exchange Online reportedly kept working.

The disruption also reached third parties. OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group postponed its third-quarter results to November 16.

Microsoft says the outage is not the result of a cyberattack. Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna confirmed it was not caused by a security breach, Business Standard reported.

## What Administrators Should Do

The fault sits in Microsoft’s infrastructure, so local troubleshooting will not restore service. Administrators should:

- Track MO1550821 and EX1550543 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, or use status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center will not load.
- Avoid resetting passwords, rebuilding Outlook profiles, or changing tenant settings in response to the errors.
- Expect intermittent access even in regions showing recovery, since Microsoft is deliberately blocking some traffic types.
- Warn users about phishing emails and fake support calls that exploit the outage.
- Plan for delayed mail delivery once service returns and queued messages are processed.:

Update 1: Microsoft is evaluating traffic throttling, protocol adjustments and failover routing to increase frontend server capacity and improve stability. The company is also expanding testing in a controlled environment to improve traffic monitoring and issue detection.

Microsoft said it is not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage. Recovery remains a priority, and the company plans to publish a post-incident report detailing the root cause and further safeguards once the disruption is mitigated.

We will update this story as Microsoft shares more on the root cause and recovery.

Microsoft has reported further progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services, with recovery actions completed across portions of the impacted infrastructure and user traffic gradually being restored.

The company confirmed improvements in key services, including Exchange Online mailbox access and delayed email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent disruptions. Engineers are now expanding recovery measures to the remaining affected infrastructure while working to stabilize services and increase server capacity to ensure consistent performance.

Microsoft has reported further progress in restoring affected Microsoft 365 services, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across an increasing portion of the impacted infrastructure.

However, some users may continue to experience intermittent disruptions as recovery efforts remain underway. Engineers are now focusing on restoring the remaining affected environments while prioritizing the reduction of queued emails and delivery backlogs.

Microsoft has also maintained an extended 48-hour email timeout window to help prevent delayed messages from expiring while email processing catches up. The company has not yet confirmed full service restoration, with further updates available under incident ID MO1550821

The post Microsoft 365 Massive Outage – Fixes Fail as Restored Servers Keep Going Unresponsive appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: CISA Warns of Google Chromium 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
articles.summary: CISA has added a new Google Chromium zero-day CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and says attackers are already using it.
articles.content:
CISA has added a new Google Chromium zero-day CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and says attackers are already using it.

It sits in the browser’s XML component and could let a remote attacker run code through a specially crafted webpage. Anyone who uses Chrome, Edge, or Opera should check their browser version today.

CISA added the flaw to the catalog on November 10, 2026, in an alert covering six new entries. The agency calls it a use-after-free bug. It says a remote attacker could run arbitrary code inside the browser sandbox.

Because the code sits in Chromium, the same weakness could affect other browsers built on it, including Microsoft Edge and Opera. CISA has not said whether ransomware groups use the flaw, and the entry lists it as unknown.

A use-after-free error happens when a program keeps using memory after it has been released. MITRE’s CWE-416 entry explains that the memory may later be reused by other code, so the old pointer now points to something it should not touch.

Attackers who control what lands in that spot can crash the browser or run their own code. The weakness is common in languages like C and C++, where developers manage memory by hand.

## Google Chromium 0-Day Actively Exploited

In this case, a victim would only need to open a booby-trapped page. CISA says the code runs inside the sandbox, which is the browser’s safety box. That does not prove a full takeover of the computer. Attackers often pair a bug like this with a second flaw to break out of the sandbox, though nothing public shows that happened here.

Google shipped the patch on November 9, 2026. Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 covers Windows and Mac, and 157.0.8103.50 covers Linux. An anonymous researcher reported the flaw on November 6, just three days before the fix arrived.

Google said it knows an exploit exists in the wild but shared nothing about who is using it, who was hit, or how. The update was one of nine security fixes in the release, and Extended Stable users should install version 156.0.8078.96.

SecurityWeek counts this as the eighth Chrome zero-day exploited this year. You can read our earlier coverage in Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely.

Memory bugs are a steady source of browser zero-days. CISA notes that Google’s own Chromium team finds that around 70% of its serious security bugs are memory safety problems.

Our review of last year’s cases, Chrome Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited in 2025, found eight exploited flaws, all added to the KEV catalog.

Open Chrome, go to Settings, then About Chrome, and let the update finish. Chrome downloads fixes in the background, but the patch only works after a restart. Make sure the version number reads 157.0.8103.50 or higher.

Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi users should install their vendor’s update as soon as it appears, since fix dates for those browsers are not yet confirmed.

IT teams should check which machines are exposed to the internet, push the update across managed devices, and confirm the browsers were actually restarted. The official KEV catalog and the CVE record will carry more detail as it becomes public.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse Cruciferra Malware-as-a-Service to Conceal Infostealers and Remote Access Trojans
articles.summary: Cybercriminals are renting a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) tool called Cruciferra to hide infostealers and remote access trojans (RATs) from security software.
articles.content:
Cybercriminals are renting a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) tool called Cruciferra to hide infostealers and remote access trojans (RATs) from security software.

The service wraps harmful files in layers of encryption, so antivirus and endpoint detection tools struggle to spot them. It is now active in many campaigns around the world.

Cruciferra is a “crypter,” a tool that scrambles a malicious file and unpacks it only when it runs on a victim’s computer. Buyers pay a monthly fee, and Proofpoint reports prices from $450 to $2,000 depending on the features.

The seller has advertised it on underground forums since fall 2025, which makes it easy for even low-skilled criminals to use.

ESET Research noted that the service has been busy. Since January 2026, ESET says it has blocked over 700,000 compromise attempts linked to Cruciferra.

Türkiye, Greece, and Spain were hit hardest. ESET also found that the service, sold since October 2025, is a rebrand of the long-running KGB cryptor, so its operators are not beginners.

## Hackers Abuse Cruciferra Malware-as-a-Service

The crypter’s best trick is its payload protection. Proofpoint found more than 90 encryption routines, most built from pieces of well-known algorithms. Each batch of samples looks different from the last, which breaks signature-based detection.

Researchers also say Cruciferra seems to be an umbrella name for several crypters sold in one package. Infections start with an email, a fake tax page, or a link to an archive. The victim opens a ZIP file holding an executable and a DLL.

Cruciferra always runs through DLL side-loading, so the clean executable quietly loads the malicious DLL. Before doing anything else, it checks for a sandbox or an analyst’s virtual machine.

The DLL is also stuffed with hundreds or thousands of fake exported functions to slow down researchers. This is similar to the crypter that can kill EDR that our team covered earlier.

Next, it goes after the defenses on the machine. Cruciferra removes the monitoring hooks that security tools place in Windows functions, hides console windows, and turns off Windows notification pop-ups.

It also drops a signed but vulnerable driver, often GoFlyDrv.sys, and uses it to shut down EDR processes. This is called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), a method many groups are now abusing trusted Windows drivers to use.

If it lacks admin rights, it bypasses the UAC prompt and adds a Run key named “putty” so it survives a reboot. The final step is a custom form of Process Ghosting. The malware writes the payload to a temporary file, marks the file for deletion, and maps it into memory.

It then starts a legitimate process and points it at the payload. Windows deletes the file, so scanners find nothing to check. Cruciferra also patches memory-query hooks and weakens the NtManageHotPatch function, which would otherwise help check the loaded image.

## Campaigns and Payloads

Proofpoint has seen dozens of campaigns from several unrelated groups. Targeting is opportunistic, with message volumes from a few hundred to thousands.

Financial, healthcare, and government groups appear most often. One actor, TA4922, sent tax-themed emails that posed as India’s Income Tax Department and led to fake portals hosting ZIP files. The result was AsyncRAT.

Other emails posed as the U.S. Social Security Administration and delivered XWorm, while guest-complaint lures aimed at hotels and travel firms led to zgRAT.

The payload list is long. It includes Agent Tesla, AsyncRAT, DarkCloud Stealer, Formbook, XLoader, Phantom Stealer, Remcos, Snake Keylogger, ValleyRAT, XWorm, and zgRAT.

Other delivery routes exist too. eSentire saw Cruciferra delivered through ClickFix pages made by the ErrTraffic MaaS tool. In that case the loader used the DCRCVDrv.sys driver to end 145 antivirus and EDR-related processes, and it dropped the Remus stealer. eSentire also describes a $1,200 monthly package and a cheaper $650 option.

Defenders should block known vulnerable drivers and keep Microsoft’s vulnerable-driver protections on. Teams should also watch for unexpected driver services, DLL side-loading from archives, and a “putty” Run key.

PowerShell logging helps, and staff should be wary of unexpected tax or complaint emails. Because pasting commands from a web page is a common trick in fake CAPTCHA lure campaigns, users should never do it.

## Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.title: Grok AI App Builder Exposes Over 35,000 Apps, Leaking Confidential Business Data and Passwords
articles.summary: Researchers found that apps built with Grok’s app builder are open to Anyone online. Thousands of these apps hold private business data, staff details, plain-text passwords, and patient information. No hacking was needed to reach them.
articles.content:
Researchers found that apps built with Grok’s app builder are open to Anyone online. Thousands of these apps hold private business data, staff details, plain-text passwords, and patient information. No hacking was needed to reach them.

Grok’s Build mode creates and publishes chat-generated apps under grok.me, while its parent company, SpaceXSI (formerly xAI), did not respond to Claroc but answered media questions on November 10, 2026.

On November 8, 2026, Claroc researchers worked through a list of more than 43,500 grok.me addresses. They opened the first page of each app once, signed in to nothing, like any visitor in a private browser window. Of the 37,571 apps still online, 35,578 (94.7%) opened for Anyone. Only 1,993 asked for a sign-in.

The list came from passive DNS, a service that records website name lookups and lets Anyone search them. Each Grok app gets its own address, so the name enters those records once someone opens the app.

## Grok AI App Builder Exposes Data

The researchers say Grok’s four-random-word names are hard to guess, but nobody needs to guess them because the records list them. The same method exposed Meta’s Muse, as covered in our Meta Muse AI privacy flaw report.

Most open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators. About one in ten held sensitive or internal data, and roughly 2% were serious enough to rate high or critical.

Confirmed examples include an intensive care briefing with a patient’s labs and ventilator status, a hospital group’s roster of more than 3,500 employees, and a fire department’s shift board with badge numbers. One contractor’s timesheet app held 18 staff accounts with plain-text passwords in code that every visitor’s browser downloads.

SpaceXSI and X staff also left 24 apps open. They included a confidential onboarding plan, a sales map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals, one aimed at a U.S. federal agency.

Another 30 identifiable organizations had internal data exposed. Of these, 26 have over 1,000 employees, and six are Fortune 500 companies. SpaceXSI took down its own 24 apps after the report, but not those of other users.

Claroc found that paid-account apps defaulted to public link access, allowing anyone to view and add records to apps without login protection.

A team app with Google sign-in checked who the visitor was but not whether they belonged to the team. A stranger with a Google account could read, edit, and delete customer records. The researchers tested this only on their own apps.

SpaceXSI says apps stay private until the creator shares them, and that publishing takes several steps. Claroc replies that every owner of the 35,578 open apps went through those same steps.

Teams should find out which AI app builders their staff use, since tools like Lovable, Replit, and Grok need no IT approval. Check each app’s access settings, and test sign-in with an outside account. Look in the app’s script files for passwords and unpublish anything nobody owns. Unpublishing a grok.me app takes it offline within seconds.

This is not Grok’s first exposure problem. In 2025, more than 370,000 shared Grok chats appeared in Google search, which we covered in our report on Grok chats exposed in Google results. The comprehensive research is on the Claroc blog.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

articles.title: Claude Code AI Discovers Technique to Turn Dormant Model Neurons Into Hidden Malware Triggers
articles.summary: Claude Code helped uncover a technique that can turn an otherwise capable AI model into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 dormant neurons.
articles.content:
Claude Code helped uncover a technique that can turn an otherwise capable AI model into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 dormant neurons.

Called Lazarus, the method plants a hidden backdoor in model weights, allowing an attacker’s trigger to make an AI agent produce commands that download and run malicious code.

The model can still pass standard evaluations and behave normally during routine tasks. The findings expose a security gap for organizations giving AI agents access to terminals, files, and credentials.

Unlike the malicious Claude Code extension reported separately, this technique does not depend on adding a malicious software loader.

Instead, the dangerous behavior sits inside the model’s internal parameters, where ordinary application security checks may miss it.

## Claude Code AI Discovers Technique

Microsoft researchers identified the Lazarus backdoor technique and detailed its malware-execution risk in research published on November 10, 2026.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence stressed that it had not observed threat actors weaponizing the method. This is a demonstrated research attack, not a confirmed malware campaign, and Claude Code was the research assistant used to discover much of the technique.

According to Microsoft’s original research explanation, principal researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos asked Claude Code, running Opus 4.5, to explore backdooring a model by hardwiring selected activations without training.

The experiment developed into a broader study, with human researchers investigating the results and defenses. Lazarus targets neurons that rarely activate during normal operation.

Researchers repurpose these quiet components as trigger detectors, using patterns already represented inside the pretrained model. A small set of examples helps separate inputs containing a chosen trigger from ordinary inputs, avoiding the cost of retraining the entire model.

This differs from prompt injection attacks bypassing safeguards through hostile instructions: Lazarus changes the model itself before deployment.

Its trigger can be an ordinary string appearing in the agent’s context, including information returned by a tool. The attacker must first obtain write access to the model checkpoint containing its weights.

Each modified neuron can push one selected token into the residual stream, the internal pathway carrying information toward the model’s next output.

Chaining several neurons lets the backdoor produce a complete command. Execution then depends on the surrounding agent software, available tools, and permissions; the model alone does not automatically control the host.

In one example, a date change into 2027 activates the hidden behavior during an ordinary task. The agent emits a command that fetches and runs attacker-controlled code.

Microsoft says the editing process needs only inference-level computing resources: hardware capable of running the model can also support this form of tampering.

## Detecting Hidden Model Changes and Limiting Damage

The central defensive challenge is that normal answers do not establish model integrity. Earlier work on detecting backdoor attacks before deployment addresses the broader problem of models that behave correctly until triggered.

Lazarus reinforces why behavioral evaluations should accompany, rather than replace, direct inspection of model weights. Microsoft recommends comparing every checkpoint against its declared original model before deployment and after updates.

Legitimate modifications generally produce broader changes, while these implants can leave unusually large edits concentrated in a few weight vectors. Advanced AI agents can help flag suspicious structures, although Microsoft cautions that no audit guarantees safe behavior.

Organizations should obtain models from original publishers, verify published file hashes, and keep approved checkpoints in access-controlled registries.

Microsoft also distinguishes conventional model scanning from weight auditing: checks for embedded malware, unsafe operators, or exposed secrets do not replace examination of altered neural parameters.

Containment remains essential because a triggered agent inherits its existing access. The same principle underlies Ghostjacking attacks against agents, where manipulated inputs can lead to dangerous tool use.

Microsoft recommends least privilege, isolated code execution, restricted outbound connections, and human approval for consequential actions. Monitoring should also cover suspicious child processes and unexpected network activity.

## Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.title: Binance Warns iPhone Users of Major iOS Flaw That May Expose Crypto Wallet, Private Keys
articles.summary: Binance has warned iPhone users about worse_query, an iOS flaw that could let malicious apps read files belonging to other apps. In its November 10 warning, the exchange named iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 as affected, saying seed phrases, private key
articles.content:
Binance has warned iPhone users about worse_query, an iOS flaw that could let malicious apps read files belonging to other apps. In its November 10 warning, the exchange named iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 as affected, saying seed phrases, private keys, and login details could be exposed.

The company said this is an operating system issue, not a flaw unique to Binance. The warning concerns the boundary that normally keeps each app’s private files separate. If an attacker crosses that boundary, sensitive data stored by wallets and other apps could become accessible.

## iOS crypto wallet vulnerability

Researcher forcequitOS published worse_query as a developer proof of concept. Its documentation describes a sandbox escape for iOS 26.0 through 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2. A sandbox is the restricted space that limits what an app can access, including files held by other apps.

The project lists access to application data folders, shared App Group folders, and some system locations. It requires an App Group container, a shared storage area linked to an app. The researcher calls it a proof of concept that “isn’t useful by itself,” rather than a complete theft tool.

Cybersecurity News previously covered iOS sandbox escape fixes that addressed similar failures in app isolation. However, those earlier patches do not establish that worse_query is fixed.

For this flaw, the key concern is whether another app’s readable files contain secrets that should remain protected.

The worse_query research repository documents file access, not confirmed cryptocurrency theft. SlowMist security chief 23pds separately warned that untrusted IPA packages could use this access to expose wallet recovery phrases, keystores, or browser cache data stored without encryption. The flaw does not automatically drain wallets.

That distinction matters. Access to a wallet’s files does not necessarily reveal usable private keys. Risk depends on what the wallet saves and how it protects those records.

Binance recommends deleting apps from untrusted sources, including sideloaded or manually signed IPA files, and updating iOS and installed apps. Anyone who suspects a breach should move funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset active login sessions.

Apple’s security release page lists iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3 updates released November 9. However, that listing alone does not confirm a worse_query fix. Users should install official updates without treating an update as proof that previously exposed wallet secrets are safe.

articles.title: SAP Security Patch Day – Critical SAP NetWeaver, Dispatcher and Gateway Vulnerabilities Patched
articles.summary: SAP’s November 2026 Security Patch Day brings fixes for critical vulnerabilities across SAP NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Gateway, and other business applications.
articles.content:
SAP’s November 2026 Security Patch Day brings fixes for critical vulnerabilities across SAP NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Gateway, and other business applications.

Released on November 10, the update includes 35 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories, and three updates to earlier notes.

Four vulnerabilities carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, making them the leading priorities for security teams. The release addresses memory corruption, missing authentication, broken access control, and code injection flaws.

SAP urges customers to review its security support portal and apply relevant corrections promptly. Administrators should check individual notes for affected components, patch requirements, and deployment instructions.

Among the most serious issues is CVE-2026-76964, a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP’s Internet Communication Manager.

According to the published CVE record, the software does not properly validate certain network input. An attacker without credentials could send crafted traffic, trigger memory corruption, and potentially execute arbitrary code, fully compromising the affected system.

## SAP Security Patch Day

SAP Security Note 3778530 addresses this vulnerability. Affected releases include KRNL64UC 7.53 and KERNEL versions 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, and 9.20. Its CVSS vector indicates network access, low attack complexity, and no privilege or user interaction requirement.

Another maximum-severity flaw, CVE-2026-89126, affects SAP Web Dispatcher and is covered by Note 3778556. The memory corruption issue spans several kernel, Web Dispatcher, HDB, and runtime components. CVE-2026-89103 addresses broken access control in SAP Gateway and is covered by Note 3798345.

The fourth 10.0-rated issue, CVE-2026-120017, involves missing authentication in the SAML2 Service Provider within SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform.

Note 3849308 covers affected SAP_BASIS releases from selected older versions through 922. All four listed vectors indicate that exploitation requires neither credentials nor user interaction.

Three further critical notes carry scores of 9.9. These cover CVE-2026-109803 in NetWeaver Knowledge Management XML Forms, CVE-2026-76965 in the ABAP Application Server, and CVE-2026-109795 in S4CRM. Their listed vectors require low-level privileges, distinguishing them from the four unauthenticated maximum-severity issues.

SAP also patched cross-site request forgery in Web Dispatcher and Internet Communication Manager, rated 9.6, and an XML external entity vulnerability in BusinessObjects Web Intelligence, rated 9.1.

Developers should also review the GitHub advisories. These include improper JWT signature verification in SAP Cloud SDK for Python versions below 0.63.1, path traversal in its Agent Memory module, and a cross-tenant sandbox takeover issue in SAP/astonish.

The release follows October’s SAP security updates, which also addressed critical code injection and access control weaknesses. Earlier September SAP patches covered additional NetWeaver and cloud risks, reinforcing the need to track successive monthly fixes rather than treat each release separately.

Security teams should match installed component versions against the November notes, prioritize reachable systems affected by critical flaws, and test patches before deploying to production.

The supplied bulletin does not report active exploitation. Severity scores describe technical risk, not evidence that attackers have already compromised vulnerable installations.

ar.summary: SAP’s November 2026 Security Patch Day brings fixes for critical vulnerabilities across SAP NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Gateway, and other business applications.
ar.content:
SAP’s November 2026 Security Patch Day brings fixes for critical vulnerabilities across SAP NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Gateway, and other business applications.

Released on November 10, the update includes 35 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories, and three updates to earlier notes.

Four vulnerabilities carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, making them the leading priorities for security teams. The release addresses memory corruption, missing authentication, broken access control, and code injection flaws.

SAP urges customers to review its security support portal and apply relevant corrections promptly. Administrators should check individual notes for affected components, patch requirements, and deployment instructions.

Among the most serious issues is CVE-2026-76964, a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP’s Internet Communication Manager.

According to the published CVE record, the software does not properly validate certain network input. An attacker without credentials could send crafted traffic, trigger memory corruption, and potentially execute arbitrary code, fully compromising the affected system.

## SAP Security Patch Day

SAP Security Note 3778530 addresses this vulnerability. Affected releases include KRNL64UC 7.53 and KERNEL versions 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, and 9.20. Its CVSS vector indicates network access, low attack complexity, and no privilege or user interaction requirement.

Another maximum-severity flaw, CVE-2026-89126, affects SAP Web Dispatcher and is covered by Note 3778556. The memory corruption issue spans several kernel, Web Dispatcher, HDB, and runtime components. CVE-2026-89103 addresses broken access control in SAP Gateway and is covered by Note 3798345.

The fourth 10.0-rated issue, CVE-2026-120017, involves missing authentication in the SAML2 Service Provider within SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform.

Note 3849308 covers affected SAP_BASIS releases from selected older versions through 922. All four listed vectors indicate that exploitation requires neither credentials nor user interaction.

Three further critical notes carry scores of 9.9. These cover CVE-2026-109803 in NetWeaver Knowledge Management XML Forms, CVE-2026-76965 in the ABAP Application Server, and CVE-2026-109795 in S4CRM. Their listed vectors require low-level privileges, distinguishing them from the four unauthenticated maximum-severity issues.

SAP also patched cross-site request forgery in Web Dispatcher and Internet Communication Manager, rated 9.6, and an XML external entity vulnerability in BusinessObjects Web Intelligence, rated 9.1.

Developers should also review the GitHub advisories. These include improper JWT signature verification in SAP Cloud SDK for Python versions below 0.63.1, path traversal in its Agent Memory module, and a cross-tenant sandbox takeover issue in SAP/astonish.

The release follows October’s SAP security updates, which also addressed critical code injection and access control weaknesses. Earlier September SAP patches covered additional NetWeaver and cloud risks, reinforcing the need to track successive monthly fixes rather than treat each release separately.

Security teams should match installed component versions against the November notes, prioritize reachable systems affected by critical flaws, and test patches before deploying to production.

The supplied bulletin does not report active exploitation. Severity scores describe technical risk, not evidence that attackers have already compromised vulnerable installations.

articles.title: Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records
articles.summary: A jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent spent more than two weeks breaking into a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its systems. It reportedly reached millions of healthcare records along the way.
articles.content:
A jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent spent more than two weeks breaking into a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its systems. It reportedly reached millions of healthcare records along the way.

Researchers at Malbear Labs call the campaign “Operation Snowball.” They found it after a routine sweep turned up an open directory holding the attacker’s full workspace.

## Jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent Breach

According to technical research published by Malbear Labs, the open directory needed no password. Inside were about 70 session transcripts, scan results for hundreds of hosts, stolen credentials and database dumps. Everything the operator typed and every report the agents wrote back was in Chinese.

The researchers did not publish the server’s IP address, which protects the victims. They also warn that the operator’s language does not prove nationality or any link to a government.

The setup was a custom agent framework built on DeepSeek Flash, a model with a one-million-token context window. That window let the main agent keep every host, password and failed attempt in memory for days. A human attacker has to re-read notes after each break. This agent did not.

DeepSeek normally refuses to write webshells or guess passwords. The operator got around this with a 78,000-character system prompt. It began with a public jailbreak template called “Little Code Sauce,” which spread through a plugin community on a Chinese forum.

The operator removed its roleplay tricks and added about 400 lines of attack instructions. The prompt told the model that a refusal was a malfunction and gave it a list of refusal phrases to avoid in English and Chinese.

This matches what other teams have seen. Palo Alto’s Unit 42 reported that a hacker named BUGSTER used a jailbroken DeepSeek V4 with the Hermes Agent framework.

That actor stole more than 5,200 records from an Indian university, and the jailbreak was only a simple system-prompt override. You can read our earlier coverage of that case for the full timeline.

The agent ran tasks from scouting to data theft with very little help. It scanned networks, tested passwords, deployed webshells and moved between systems. When defenses blocked it, it changed course.

Reports say it wrote its own replacement tunneling tool and rebuilt an exploit chain against a locked-down Liferay server.

The operator’s messages were very short. One was “Go on,” and another told the agent to close up the latest high-risk hole. The agent chose the target, the flaw and the method. A person running this does not need to understand the techniques.

The harness also scored every break-in, like a game. A pivot into a separate internal network segment earned far more points than a single server shell. Security tools such as firewall consoles also scored high.

At the time of recovery the total was 3,725 points. The scoring shows the operator cared most about the systems that watch and divide a network.

The most worrying finding involves healthcare data. Default login details reportedly gave the agent full database admin access to a TrakCare system running on an old Oracle 9i database.

That exposed millions of records across patient, vaccination and appointment tables. The agent also pulled thousands of rows of subscriber billing and device data and took cryptographic keys from the telecom.

One caution applies. A summary of the report notes that these outcomes were not independently verified in the material available. Treat the exact scale as the researchers’ claim for now.

Even so, the root cause is basic, because an unchanged default password opened the door.

This campaign is not a one-off. CrowdStrike reported that the China-linked group VAPOR PANDA ran the ARTEX framework, mostly on DeepSeek, against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries over 11 days starting October 17.

It confirmed access at nine organizations, where the group planted the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor. Telecom providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also hit.

Speed is a big change here. CrowdStrike’s Adam Meyers said human intruders usually run up to 40 commands an hour, while ARTEX activity passed 1,500. Our own report on how ARTEX automates enterprise attacks explains the framework in more detail.

Because no human sits at the keyboard, hunting for working-hours patterns or slow, careful sessions will not help. The agent’s activity is loud and repetitive, so watch endpoint and network logs for fast scanning, bursts of failed logins and unusual tunnels.

Start with the basics:

- Change every default password, especially on old database systems.
- Keep internal network segments truly separate.
- Place endpoint sensors on servers that seem unreachable from the internet.
- Keep an eye on open directories and exposed storage.

The lesson is simple. AI did not invent new weaknesses. It found the old ones faster than any team can patch them.

articles.title: Hackers Used Default admin:admin Credentials to Exploit ForgeRock RCE and Remotely Unlock Cars
articles.summary: Researchers used default admin:admin credentials as part of a vulnerability chain that let them run code on two automakers’ production ForgeRock servers and remotely unlock connected cars.
articles.content:
Researchers used default admin:admin credentials as part of a vulnerability chain that let them run code on two automakers’ production ForgeRock servers and remotely unlock connected cars.

Found in early 2026 and disclosed on November 7, the flaws also exposed vehicle locations and supported remote engine commands.

The findings came from controlled security research, not a reported criminal campaign. Both unnamed automakers fixed the issue within about two hours of receiving the report and rotated affected credentials. Their identity systems served multiple regions, but the researchers tested the complete account takeover and vehicle access chain only with US accounts and vehicles.

## ForgeRock Attack Chain

The investigation began with the Android apps used by vehicle owners. Both apps relied on ForgeRock Access Management for login sessions and OpenIDM for customer records. Tracing an email validation request led the researchers toward administrative services, including the Apache Felix Web Console running alongside OpenIDM.

A web application firewall blocked direct requests to those services. However, specially encoded paths made requests appear to target static files while Jetty, the backend web server, interpreted them as console requests. This mismatch in URL handling exposed the hidden management interface, where the documented default username and password still worked.

Access to Felix’s ConfigMgr interface allowed the researchers to create an OpenIDM scheduled task that ran Groovy code. They used it to install a small Java component inside the running service, giving them a controlled command endpoint. This confirmed remote code execution within the production identity process rather than inside the cars themselves.

## From Server Access to Vehicle Commands

According to the researchers’ technical report, server access exposed administrative credentials that allowed local requests to customer records. The team changed a test account’s email and password, received its verification codes, and completed the normal login process. They then exchanged the session for tokens accepted by the vehicle APIs.

Those tokens exposed the account’s vehicles, location, status, and supported remote controls. With the owner beside the test vehicle, Shah confirmed unlocking, engine start, engine stop, and locking.

Restoring the original email did not cancel the new tokens. The findings follow earlier Kia remote access research and Subaru STARLINK security flaws.

Ping Identity’s production hardening guide already advises removing or protecting the Felix console and changing its default credentials. It also warns that console authentication is separate from IDM authentication. The case shows why blocking administrative URLs at a firewall cannot replace securing the service behind it, especially when that service controls customer identity and access to connected vehicles.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

Found in early 2026 and disclosed on November 7, the flaws also exposed vehicle locations and supported remote engine commands.

The findings came from controlled security research, not a reported criminal campaign. Both unnamed automakers fixed the issue within about two hours of receiving the report and rotated affected credentials. The investigation began with the Android apps used by vehicle owners. Both apps relied on ForgeRock Access Management for login sessions and OpenIDM for customer records. Tracing an email validation request led the researchers toward administrative services, including the Apache Felix Web Console running alongside OpenIDM.

A web application firewall blocked direct requests to those services. However, specially encoded paths made requests appear to target static files while Jetty, the backend web server, interpreted them as console requests. This mismatch in URL handling exposed the hidden management interface, where the documented default username and password still worked.

Access to Felix’s ConfigMgr interface allowed the researchers to create an OpenIDM scheduled task that ran Groovy code. articles.title: SonicWall Warns of Potential In-the-Wild Exploitation of SSLVPN Flaw That Bypasses MFA
articles.summary: SonicWall has warned customers to patch a SonicOS SSLVPN vulnerability that could let attackers bypass SAML authentication and its multi-factor authentication checks.
articles.content:
SonicWall has warned customers to patch a SonicOS SSLVPN vulnerability that could let attackers bypass SAML authentication and its multi-factor authentication checks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-19868, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 7.1. The company has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation and strongly urges customers to upgrade promptly.

The issue affects SSLVPN only when SAML is enabled for logins. An attacker must have valid credentials for an alternate authentication method, making this different from a login bypass that requires no account. Under affected conditions, those credentials may allow access without passing the SAML controls intended to protect the connection.

SAML lets organizations use a central identity provider to handle user sign-ins. Here, the weakness concerns authentication enforcement through another login method, rather than a stated flaw in SAML itself.

Successful exploitation may also skip MFA enforced through SAML, leaving a gap between the security policy administrators expect and the checks actually applied.

Ryan Harris of The Electronic Office reported the vulnerability. SonicWall includes it among seven issues in its latest advisory. Although the exploitation warning raises urgency, the supplied details do not identify attackers, victims, attack dates, or the scale of activity. Describing a confirmed widespread campaign would therefore go beyond the available evidence.

Earlier SonicWall SSLVPN authentication bypass coverage shows why remote access flaws deserve attention. However, that reporting concerns CVE-2024-53704, a separate vulnerability.

Its session-hijacking behavior should not be treated as evidence of how CVE-2026-19868 works or what attackers have done with this newly disclosed issue.

## SonicOS SSLVPN Vulnerability Exploited

The SonicWall security advisory, published November 6, also lists CVE-2026-107155 and CVE-2026-107154. Both score 8.8 and affect the management interface. They involve a permissive cross-domain policy and session validation, respectively, and could permit unauthorized operations under specific conditions. Their vectors include required user interaction.

CVE-2026-82308 is a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow in SSLVPN, rated 7.5. CVE-2026-77708 and CVE-2026-77709 affect the TACACS+ authentication client, and each scores 5.9. These flaws could cause application-level denial of service. CVE-2026-19703, rated 5.2, could expose a limited platform credential on virtual appliances to an attacker with existing local access.

Affected releases include Gen7 hardware and NSv appliances running SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 or earlier, and Gen8 hardware and NSv appliances running 8.2.2-8015 or earlier. SonicWall lists fixes in 7.3.4-7013 and later for Gen7, and 8.2.3-8015 and later for Gen8. No workaround is listed.

Administrators should prioritize patching, confirm their appliance generation, and install the matching fixed release. Previous SonicOS vulnerability reporting covers different flaws and firmware fixes, so older patch guidance should not replace this advisory’s requirements. Review enabled authentication methods and check VPN login activity while completing the upgrade.

articles.content:
Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js

Insignary, a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js.

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely.

Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases.

Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution.

The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued.

insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the –fix option.

It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify.

Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package.

End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release.

Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention.

The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image.

insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code.

Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning.

Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s –clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server.

“PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary.

“We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.”

insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker.

It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported.

Insignary Inc. is a Toronto-based cybersecurity company specializing in binary composition analysis and software supply chain security.

Its patented technology enables organizations to identify open-source software components, vulnerabilities, and software provenance directly from compiled binaries without requiring access to source code.

The company serves enterprises, governments, and software vendors worldwide and is backed by strategic investors and partners including BearingPoint in Europe, Cybertrust Japan and TechMatrix in Japan, and TMA Solutions.

Through its global partner ecosystem, Insignary supports software supply chain security initiatives across North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information, visit www.insignary.com.

Principal Solutions Architect

ru.title: Insignary Releases Free Insignary-Chk Tool to Detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell Exposure
ru.summary: Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js
ru.content:
Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js

Insignary, a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js.

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely.

Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed.

The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases.

Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution.

The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued.

insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the –fix option.

It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify.

Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package.

End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release.

Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention.

The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image.

insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code.

Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning.

Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s –clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server.

“PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary.

“We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.”

insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker.

It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported.
